steps: This video shows how hooks enforce policy on tool calls. Your code registers two hooks on the tool gate: pre tool use matching Bash, and post tool use with no matcher, so it sees every call.
Asked to clean the build folder, Claude reaches for r m dash r f build, and emits a Bash tool use toward the gate.
Pre tool use fires before permissions are checked. The block dangerous hook sees r m dash r f and returns a deny decision. The Bash tool never runs.
The error tells Claude why it was blocked, so it picks a safe alternative and asks to run l s build instead.
No r m dash r f this time, so the hook returns an empty object, meaning no objection. The gate lets the command run, and Bash lists the build files.
Post tool use fires only for the call that actually ran. One audit line is written for the l s, and none for the blocked delete.

The result reaches Claude, which reports the build folder was inspected safely. Hooks enforce rules in code, where a prompt could only ask nicely. The full walkthrough is in the Gennoor Claude certification course.
